1.pericope_label: After two days was the feast of the passover, and of unleavened bread: and the chief priests and the scribes sought how they might take him by craft, and put him to death. But they said, Not on the feast day, lest there be an uproar of the people.

schools.summary: Gill dates the scene by what precedes it and explains the feast by its origin. The two days are counted from the discourse Christ had just delivered concerning the destruction of the temple at Jerusalem; the feast was kept in commemoration of God’s passing over the houses of the Israelites when he destroyed the firstborn of Egypt and made way for the deliverance of the children of Israel, and was kept by eating the passover lamb, which properly speaking is the feast of the passover. On the decision to delay he explains what the priests feared: the feast was two days off, and a great concourse of people would then be gathered from all parts to keep it.

Henry gives two reasons why the death had to fall at this feast and then anatomises the plotters. The reasons: that his death and suffering might be the more public, so that all Israel, even those of the dispersion who came from all parts to the feast, might be witnesses of it and of the wonders attending it; and that the antitype might answer to the type, since Christ our Passover was sacrificed for us and brought us out of the house of bondage at the same time that the paschal lamb was sacrificed and Israel’s deliverance out of Egypt was commemorated. On the plotters he marks first how spiteful they were, since they did not think it enough to banish or imprison him but aimed not merely to silence him and stop his progress for the future but to be revenged on him for all the good he had done; and then how subtle, since the reason they give for delay is not that the people would be diverted from their devotions but that there might be an uproar — men who desired nothing more than the praise of men dreading nothing more than their rage and displeasure.

Barnes and Robertson supply the terms and the chronology. Barnes explains the second name of the feast, so called because at it no bread was used except what had been made without leaven or yeast, and glosses the craft as subtilty — some secret plan that would secure possession of him without exciting the opposition of the people. Robertson dates the scene to Tuesday evening as we count time, the beginning of the Jewish Wednesday, notes that Matthew reports Jesus naming this same date, which would place it at our Thursday evening, and observes that John mentions five items which on a superficial view seem to contradict the definite date given here but are really in harmony with it; he adds that Mark uses both names of the feast, each covering the eight days. On the decision to delay he reconstructs a change of plan: the priests had first intended to kill Jesus at the feast, and it was the Triumphal Entry and the great debate in the temple that very morning which decided them to wait until it was over, since it had become plain that he had too large and powerful a following.

Theophylact contributes a single sentence which reverses the apparent direction of the narrative. Whatever the chief priests were contriving, Christ himself had determined for himself the day of his Passion; for he wished to be crucified at the Passover, because he was the true Passover.

Bede and Pseudo-Jerome both begin from the name of the feast, and differ over it. Bede denies the derivation from Passion which he says many assume, insisting that Pascha, the Hebrew phase, comes from passing over — either because the destroyer saw the blood on the Israelites’ doors and passed by without smiting them, or because the Lord himself, bringing aid to his people, walked above them. He then distinguishes the two feasts precisely: under the Old Testament the name Passover belonged to the single day on which the lamb was slain in the evening, the fourteenth moon of the first month, while the feast of unleavened bread began at the fifteenth, the day they came out of Egypt. Pseudo-Jerome accepts passing over as the sense of phase but holds that Pascha means sacrifice, and treats the opening of the chapter as an occasion for ritual language rather than exposition: let us sprinkle our book and our thresholds with blood, put the scarlet thread about the house of our prayers and bind scarlet on our hand as was done to Zarah, so that we may say the red heifer is slain in the valley — for the Evangelist, being about to speak of the slaying of Christ, premises the two days before the Passover.

debates: Where the name Pascha comes from. Bede rejects the derivation from Passion as a common error and refers it to the passing over; Pseudo-Jerome grants that sense for the Hebrew phase but holds that Pascha itself means sacrifice. The two stand in the same chain and are not reconciled.

Why the priests resolved not to act during the feast. Henry and Barnes take it as fear of an uproar and a preference for a secret seizure; Gill explains the fear from the size of the festival crowd; Robertson makes it a reversal of an earlier plan, forced on them by the Triumphal Entry and the temple debate of that morning.

Who fixed the time of the death. Theophylact and Henry both say Christ did, Theophylact because he was the true Passover and Henry because the type required it and the publicity served it; Robertson and Barnes describe only the priests’ deliberations, and Robertson has them settling on a date they did not in the event keep.
outliers: Pseudo-Jerome alone opens the passion narrative with an exhortation rather than an explanation, calling for blood on the thresholds and scarlet on the hand before he comes to the text at all.
Bede alone sets out the calendar distinction between the single Passover day and the following feast of unleavened bread, which the others leave merged in the two names Mark gives.
themes: the feast of the passover and unleavened bread
Christ choosing the day of his Passion
the plot of the chief priests

3.pericope_label: And being in Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, as he sat at meat, there came a woman having an alabaster box of ointment of spikenard very precious; and she brake the box, and poured it on his head. And there were some that had indignation within themselves, and said, Why was this waste of the ointment made? For it might have been sold for more than three hundred pence, and have been given to the poor. And they murmured against her. And Jesus said, Let her alone; why trouble ye her? she hath wrought a good work on me. For ye have the poor with you always, and whensoever ye will ye may do them good: but me ye have not always. She hath done what she could: she is come aforehand to anoint my body to the burying. Verily I say unto you, Wheresoever this gospel shall be preached throughout the whole world, this also that she hath done shall be spoken of for a memorial of her.

schools.summary: Gill supplies the geography and the money. Bethany lay about two miles from Jerusalem, and Christ retired there after taking his leave of the temple and predicting its destruction, going to and from it often in the last week of his life because he had dear friends and familiar acquaintance in the place — Lazarus and his two sisters among them. He values the three hundred pence at nine pounds, seven shillings and sixpence of English money. On the rebuke he explains what Christ was answering: knowing the secret indignation of some of his disciples, their private murmuring and their continual teasing of the woman over the expense, he told them to let her alone and cease to chide her for what she had done.

Henry reads the episode as an instance of the kindness of Christ’s friends. One friend was kind enough to invite him to supper and he kind enough to accept, since though he had a prospect of his death approaching he did not abandon himself to a melancholy retirement from all company; another was kind enough to anoint his head with very precious ointment as he sat at meat. He observes that she poured it all out, and since an alabaster box is not easily broken and need not be broken to get the ointment out, records the alternative reading that she shook the box or struck it against the ground to loosen what was in it. On the burial he draws the comparison that it is usual for those condemned to die to have their coffins prepared and other provision made for their funerals while they are yet alive, and that Christ accepted this in the same spirit — adding that he never rode in triumph into Jerusalem except when he came there to suffer, nor had his head anointed except for his burial.

Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott, Lightfoot and Robertson divide the material questions. Barnes objects that the English ‘ointment’ does not convey the proper meaning, since this was a liquid perfume used only to give a pleasant odour, and describes the nard as a plant of the East Indies with a small slender stalk and a heavy thick root, the best perfume being obtained from the root. Clarke canvasses the conjectures about the alabaster box — a glass phial, a small vessel without a handle so named from a privative and the word for handle, or simply an essence bottle — and notes that many manuscripts and versions add the word for the ointment in the next verse, a reading Griesbach received into the text. Lightfoot works from Pliny, giving both the composition of nardine and the market prices of such precious ointments, which he says were commonly known. Ellicott notes that Mark limits the murmurers to ‘some’, an intermediate stage between Matthew’s ‘the disciples’ and John’s naming of Judas; that the specific sum, absent from Matthew, is one of the few points common to Mark and John; and that the word rendered ‘good’ means noble, the higher form of goodness, its use here being peculiar to Mark. Robertson distinguishes this incident from the anointing in Luke, notes that the adjective joined to the nard occurs only here and in John, that the verb for murmuring is a striking word used of the snorting of horses, and that the ‘far above’ may be a detail preserved from Peter’s memory of the objection.

Clarke and Wesley both attend to the objectors and the sum. Wesley states plainly that those who had indignation were incited to it by Judas, and that they probably said what they said to the women rather than to Christ. Clarke, besides his account of the alabaster box, reckons the three hundred pence at nearly ten pounds sterling.

Theophylact takes up the same problem and reaches a different answer, revising it as he goes. Although the four Evangelists record an anointing by a woman, he says, there were two women and not one: the one John describes is the sister of Lazarus, who six days before the Passover anointed the feet of Jesus, and the one the other three describe is another. Then he corrects himself — on examination one will find three rather than two, since one is described by John, another by Luke, and a third by the remaining two Evangelists.

Origen states the objection and rules on it. Those present were grieved at the waste of the ointment, which might have been sold for a large sum and given to the poor; but this ought not to have been, since it was right that the ointment should be poured over the head of Christ with a holy and fitting stream. He adds that the praise of this good work is so effectual that it ought to excite all of us.

Bede, Pseudo-Jerome and Augustine take the scene as figure and as history in turn. Bede finds it fitting that the Lord, when about to suffer for the whole world and to redeem all nations with his blood, should dwell at Bethany, which is the house of obedience; and he explains the host’s title, that Simon is called the leper not because he remained one at that time but because, having once been such, he had been healed by the Saviour. Pseudo-Jerome develops the same method: the fawn among the stags returns to his couch, that is, the Son, obedient to the Father even unto death, seeks obedience from us; in a mystic sense Simon the leper is the world, at first unbelieving and afterwards converted, and the woman with the alabaster box is the faith of the Church, whose spikenard sends forth its smell — the nard being called pistic, that is, faithful and precious. Augustine addresses the historical question instead, and holds that the sinner who came to the feet of Jesus can be none other than the same Mary who did this twice, once as Luke relates when she came for the first time with humility and tears and merited the remission of her sins, an occasion John himself alludes to when introducing the raising of Lazarus.

debates: How many anointings the Gospels record. Theophylact says two, and then on examination three; Augustine says one woman, Mary, anointed Christ twice; Robertson settles only that this incident differs from the one in Luke. The chain thus contains two incompatible answers side by side.

What the objection to the waste was worth. Origen grants the calculation and rejects the conclusion, holding it right that the ointment should be poured on Christ’s head; Ellicott traces how the murmurers narrow from ‘the disciples’ to ‘some’ to Judas across the three accounts; Wesley makes Judas the instigator of the rest.

What the three hundred pence amount to. Gill gives nine pounds seven shillings and sixpence, Clarke nearly ten pounds, Barnes about forty-one dollars; Lightfoot approaches the question from the other side, by the recorded market prices of nard.

Whether the box was broken. Henry notes that alabaster is not easily broken and that breaking was unnecessary to get the ointment out, and records a reading in which she shook or struck the vessel instead.
outliers: Pseudo-Jerome alone reads every element of the scene as allegory — Simon as the world, the woman as the Church’s faith, the nard as fidelity — where even Bede, working in the same chain, allegorises only the place-name.
Lightfoot alone approaches the ointment through classical pharmacology, citing the composition of nardine and Pliny’s price list rather than the theology of the act.
themes: the house of Simon the leper
Bethany as the house of obedience
a good work wrought on Christ
a memorial wherever the gospel is preached

10.pericope_label: And Judas Iscariot, one of the twelve, went unto the chief priests, to betray him unto them. And when they heard it, they were glad, and promised to give him money. And he sought how he might conveniently betray him.

schools.summary: Gill connects the betrayal to the preceding scene and explains the priests’ gladness. Judas was the principal person who had taken indignation at the woman and murmured at the profusion of the ointment. The priests were glad that such an opportunity offered, and from such a quarter — one of Christ’s own disciples — so that the thing might be done more secretly and effectually, and with less blame to themselves.

Henry asks what Judas had that the priests wanted. What he proposed was to betray Christ to them and to give them notice when and where they might find and seize him without making an uproar among the people, which they feared if they took him in public among his admirers. Henry doubts that Judas knew where their counsels had run aground, since the debate had been held in their close cabal, and equally doubts that they had imagined any of Christ’s intimates could be so base; but Satan, who was entered into Judas, knew what occasion they had for him and could guide him to be guide to them.

Wesley and Clarke each supply a single sharp sentence. Wesley dates the visit precisely, that Judas went to the chief priests immediately after the reproof at Bethany, having anger now added to his covetousness. Clarke passes judgment on the priests rather than on Judas: the joy that arises from the opportunity of murdering an innocent person must be completely infernal.

Robertson and Ellicott confine themselves to the wording. Robertson notes the definite article, which Matthew lacks, and rejects the suggestion that Mark is here calling Judas the primate among the twelve; the article rather calls attention to his being the one of the twelve who did this deed. Ellicott makes two observations from comparison with the other Gospels: the mention of the priests being glad is in common with Luke, and Mark, unlike Matthew, does not name the specific sum promised as the price of blood.

Chrysostom and Theophylact take the naming and the plan. Chrysostom is severe about the man and careful about the Evangelist’s language: asked why the country is mentioned, he answers that he would he could have been ignorant of Judas’s existence altogether, but explains that the surname distinguishes this Judas from the other disciple of that name, the brother of James, lest confusion arise between them. He observes that the Evangelist does not write ‘Judas the traitor’, thereby teaching us to be guiltless of detraction and to avoid accusing others, while ‘one of the twelve’ enhances the guilt, since there were seventy other disciples who were not so intimate with Christ nor admitted to such familiar intercourse. Theophylact explains what the betrayal actually consisted in: to betray him unto them was to announce to them when he should be alone, since they feared to rush upon him while he was teaching, for fear of the people.

Bede and Pseudo-Jerome both fix responsibility on Judas himself. Bede supplies the motive from the preceding scene, that the unhappy man wished to compensate with the price of his Master for the loss he thought he had made by the pouring out of the ointment; and he presses the verb, since ‘he went’ shows that Judas was neither invited by the chief priests nor bound by any necessity but entered upon the design from the spontaneous wickedness of his own mind. He turns this on the reader: many shudder at the crime of selling his Master, his Lord and his God for money as monstrous and horrible wickedness, and yet do not take heed to themselves. Pseudo-Jerome reduces the matter to a series of antitheses — one of the twelve in number, not in merit; one in body, not in soul — observes that Judas went to the chief priests only after Satan had entered into him, since every living thing unites with what is like itself, and hears in his promise an echo of the devil’s own offer of all this power. On the bargain he notes that the priests promise money and lose their life, which Judas also loses on receiving it, and that no opportunity for treachery can be found which escapes vengeance here or hereafter.

debates: What moved Judas. Bede and Wesley both trace it to the rebuke over the ointment, Bede as an attempt to recover the loss and Wesley as anger added to covetousness; Gill connects him to the murmuring; Pseudo-Jerome makes Satan’s entry the decisive point rather than any grievance.

What ‘one of the twelve’ signifies. Chrysostom takes it as aggravating the guilt by contrast with the seventy; Pseudo-Jerome as marking a numerical membership without moral membership; Robertson as simple identification, and he expressly denies the reading that would make Judas the chief of the apostles.

Why the priests were glad. Gill explains it by the secrecy and deniability an insider afforded; Theophylact by their fear of seizing Christ while he taught; Clarke declines the analysis and calls the gladness itself infernal.

Whether Judas knew what the priests needed. Henry doubts it, since their deliberations were private, and doubts equally that they expected such an offer — assigning the coordination to Satan rather than to either party’s calculation.
outliers: Chrysostom alone draws a lesson in charitable speech from the Evangelist’s restraint, noting that Mark writes ‘Judas Iscariot’ and not ‘Judas the traitor’, even while saying of the man himself that he wishes he had never heard of him.
Pseudo-Jerome alone extends the sentence to the buyers as well as the seller, observing that the priests lose their life by the same transaction in which Judas loses his.
themes: betraying him when he should be alone

12.pericope_label: And the first day of unleavened bread, when they killed the passover, his disciples said unto him, Where wilt thou that we go and prepare that thou mayest eat the passover? And he sendeth forth two of his disciples, and saith unto them, Go ye into the city, and there shall meet you a man bearing a pitcher of water: follow him. And wheresoever he shall go in, say ye to the goodman of the house, The Master saith, Where is the guestchamber, where I shall eat the passover with my disciples? And he will shew you a large upper room furnished and prepared: there make ready for us. And his disciples went forth, and came into the city, and found as he had said unto them: and they made ready the passover.

schools.summary: Gill supplies the dates and the names without argument: the first day of unleavened bread is the fourteenth of Nisan, and the two disciples sent forward are Peter and John, as appears from the parallel account.

Henry attends to Christ’s own bearing on the night before he died. He ate the Passover with his disciples, and prepared himself for his approaching sorrows with the joys and comforts of that ordinance, the full prospect of what was coming not indisposing him for the solemnity. From this Henry draws a rule for others: no apprehension of trouble, whether it has come or is coming, should put us by, or put us out of frame for, our attendance on holy ordinances as we have opportunity.

Lightfoot, Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson handle chronology and comparison. Lightfoot poses the chronological difficulty as a challenge: those who hold that Christ kept his Passover on the fourteenth while the Jews deferred theirs to the fifteenth, because that year’s Passover was transferred on account of the following sabbath, must say whether the evangelists are speaking by the day Moses prescribed or by the day then observed. Barnes explains what preparing the Passover meant — to procure a lamb, have it roasted and properly furnished with the usual accompaniments — and identifies the city as Jerusalem, the party being then at Bethany about two miles off. Ellicott notes that the number of the messengers is given by Mark and their names by Luke only, and that the sign of the pitcher of water is common to Mark and Luke but not found in Matthew. Robertson takes the imperfect as marking customary practice, explains that the paschal lamb was slain at six in the evening at the beginning of the fifteenth while the preparations were made beforehand on the fourteenth, and notes the same distribution of details between Luke and Matthew.

Clarke and Wesley both read the sign of the water-carrier as evidence, and draw different conclusions from it. Clarke exclaims at the exactness of Christ’s foreknowledge, which comprehends even the minutest circumstances, and turns the detail into a doctrine of providence: an honest employment, however mean, is worthy of the attention of God, and even a man bearing a pitcher of water is marked in all his steps and is an object of the merciful regards of the Most High. Wesley makes the sign seasonable rather than exemplary, an additional proof given at the right moment both of Christ’s knowing all things and of his influence over the minds of men.

Chrysostom and Theophylact set the preparations against the plot. Chrysostom marks the contrast, that while Judas was plotting how to betray him the rest of the disciples were taking care of the preparation of the Passover — not our Passover, but for the present that of the Jews. Theophylact draws two inferences from the arrangements. From the disciples’ question, where they should go and prepare, it seems evident that Christ had no dwelling-place and that the disciples had no houses of their own, since otherwise they would have taken him there. And from his sending two of them, Peter and John as Luke names them, to a man unknown to him, Theophylact concludes that Christ might, had he so pleased, have avoided his Passion.

Bede, Pseudo-Jerome and Augustine take the calendar, the figure and a harmonising detail. Bede identifies the first day of the Passover as the fourteenth of the first month, when leaven was thrown aside and the lamb was killed at even, and observes that although Christ was crucified on the next day, the fifteenth moon, it was on the night the lamb was offered that he acted, citing the apostle’s words that Christ our Passover is sacrificed for us. Pseudo-Jerome reads the unleavened bread eaten with bitter herbs as our redemption, the bitterness being the Passion of our Lord; takes the disciples’ question as showing that we should direct our steps according to the will of God; and notes that the Lord points out with whom he would eat the Passover and, after his custom, sends two disciples. Augustine resolves the difference between the accounts of the vessel: where Mark says a pitcher, Luke says a two-handed vessel, the one pointing out the kind of vessel and the other the mode of carrying it, and both meaning the same truth.

debates: Which day is meant by the first day of unleavened bread. Bede takes it as the fourteenth, when the lamb was killed at even, and places the crucifixion on the fifteenth; Robertson distinguishes the slaying at six in the evening, beginning the fifteenth, from the preparations made on the fourteenth; Gill simply names the fourteenth of Nisan; Lightfoot refuses to settle it and instead presses those who separate Christ’s Passover from the Jews’ to say by which reckoning the evangelists speak.

What the sign of the water-carrier establishes. Clarke takes it for foreknowledge extending to the minutest circumstance, and beyond that for God’s regard to humble employments; Wesley for knowledge joined with influence over men’s minds; Theophylact for the voluntariness of the Passion, since one who could arrange this could have escaped it.

How the accounts of the vessel differ. Augustine reconciles pitcher and two-handed vessel as descriptions of kind and of carriage respectively; Ellicott and Robertson note only which Gospels carry the detail.
outliers: Theophylact alone infers homelessness from the disciples’ question, reasoning that had either Christ or they possessed a house the question could not have arisen.
Henry alone turns the occasion into a rule about public worship under the shadow of trouble, taking Christ’s composure at the Passover as the pattern.
themes: the first day of unleavened bread
a man bearing a pitcher of water
the guestchamber and the upper room

17.pericope_label: And in the evening he cometh with the twelve. And as they sat and did eat, Jesus said, Verily I say unto you, One of you which eateth with me shall betray me. And they began to be sorrowful, and to say unto him one by one, Is it I? and another said, Is it I? And he answered and said unto them, It is one of the twelve, that dippeth with me in the dish. The Son of man indeed goeth, as it is written of him: but woe to that man by whom the Son of man is betrayed! good were it for that man if he had never been born.

schools.summary: Gill reconstructs the movements of the day and corrects the posture. He supposes Christ set out from Bethany in the afternoon with the other nine and came to Jerusalem, where he was joined by Judas, who had already covenanted with the chief priests, and by Peter and John, who had been sent ahead to prepare; and that when the second evening had come he went with all twelve to the house where the provision was made. On the table he notes that the phrase means as they lay along, such being the posture at the eating of the Passover, and on the sorrow that all were sorrowful except Judas.

Clarke contributes the one textual note on the passage. The clause reporting a second questioner — ‘and another said, Is it I?’ — is wanting in a number of manuscripts and in the Syriac, Persic, Arabic, Coptic, Ethiopic, Vulgate and four copies of the Itala; Griesbach leaves the question doubtful, and others omit the clause altogether.

Ellicott, Robertson and Clarke supply translation, custom and text. Ellicott corrects ‘as they sat’ to ‘as they reclined’. Robertson presses the same correction harder, calling it a pity that these verbs are not properly translated in English and observing that even Leonardo da Vinci, in his painting of the Last Supper, has Jesus and the apostles sitting rather than reclining — probably taking an artist’s licence for effect. He places the meal at the regular hour, six in the evening at the beginning of the fifteenth, notes the dramatic historical present in the coming, and draws out the force of the phrase about eating together by remarking that to this day the Arabs will not violate hospitality by mistreating one who has broken bread with them in the tent.

Chrysostom, Theophylact and Cyril of Jerusalem take three different points. Chrysostom explains the exact degree of disclosure: Christ did not proclaim the traitor openly to all, lest he should make him the more shameless, and yet did not keep it altogether silent, lest thinking himself undiscovered he should hasten the more boldly to betray him. Theophylact raises a legal difficulty about the posture — how could they eat reclining when the law required the Passover to be eaten standing and upright? — and answers that they had probably fulfilled the legal Passover first and had reclined when Christ began to give them his own; he also explains why the disciples grew sad although none of them but one had any such intention, namely that being free of the passion they still trusted him who knows all hearts rather than their own knowledge of themselves. Cyril of Jerusalem uses the closing verse to establish that Christ came to his passion willingly: others, who do not foresee their end, die unwillingly, whereas he spoke of his passion beforehand, saying that the Son of man is betrayed to be crucified.

Bede and Pseudo-Jerome take the warning and the hour. Bede holds that the Lord, having already foretold his Passion, prophesied of the traitor as well in order to give him room for repentance, so that on understanding his thoughts were known he might turn; and he identifies Judas by his behaviour at the table, since when the others were saddened and held back their hands he put out his hand into the dish along with his Master. Pseudo-Jerome reads the hour as figure: the evening of the day points out the evening of the world, since the last, who are the first to receive the penny of eternal life, come about the eleventh hour. He then turns the disciples’ questioning into an image of music, all of them touched by the Lord so that there is among them the harmony of the harp, every well-attuned string answering with accordant tone — while one alone, unstrung and steeped in the love of money, asks the same question as the rest.

debates: Why Christ named the betrayal without naming the man. Chrysostom explains it as a deliberate middle course, avoiding both the shamelessness that open exposure would breed and the boldness that concealment would allow; Bede takes the whole warning as an offer of room for repentance.

How they could be reclining at a Passover the law required to be eaten standing. Theophylact answers that the legal Passover had already been kept and that the reclining belongs to the new one Christ was instituting; Ellicott, Robertson and Gill treat the same words as a translation problem rather than a legal one, and do not raise the difficulty at all.
Whether the second ‘Is it I?’ belongs to the text. Clarke reports it wanting in many manuscripts and versions and notes that Griesbach left it doubtful while others omitted it.

Why the disciples doubted themselves. Theophylact accounts for it by their trusting the searcher of hearts above their own self-knowledge; Gill simply records that all were sorrowful but Judas; Pseudo-Jerome makes their common question the sign of their concord and the traitor’s the one discordant note.
outliers: Robertson alone appeals to a work of art to show how far the mistranslation has shaped the imagination, citing Leonardo’s seated apostles as evidence of the error’s reach.
Pseudo-Jerome alone hears the scene as music, treating the disciples’ identical question as strings in tune and Judas as the one string unstrung.
themes: the evening meal with the twelve
one of you shall betray me
sorrow and self-distrust among the disciples
the Son of man goeth as it is written

22.pericope_label: And as they did eat, Jesus took bread, and blessed, and brake it, and gave to them, and said, Take, eat: this is my body. And he took the cup, and when he had given thanks, he gave it to them: and they all drank of it. And he said unto them, This is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many. Verily I say unto you, I will drink no more of the fruit of the vine, until that day that I drink it new in the kingdom of God.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin work on the occasion and on the purpose. Gill fixes the moment at the conclusion of the paschal lamb and unleavened bread, notes that the thanks over the cup were given both over it and for it, blessing it and appropriating it to the present use and service, and observes that the words about the blood were spoken as Christ handed the cup rather than after they had drunk of it. Calvin directs the whole to the death: the words point us to the sacrifice of Christ’s death, without the remembrance of which the Lord’s Supper is never observed in a proper manner, since it is impossible for believing souls to be satisfied in any other way than by being assured that God is pacified toward them.

Henry describes the ordinance by its use rather than by its metaphysics. The Lord’s supper is food for the soul, and therefore a very little of what is for the body — as much as will serve for a sign — is enough. It was instituted by the example and the practice of our Master, to remain in force until his second coming; it was instituted with blessing and with giving of thanks, to be a memorial of Christ’s death; and frequent mention is made of his precious blood as the price of our redemption.

Clarke contributes a textual judgment. The word for eating in the words over the bread is omitted by many manuscripts and versions, but he thinks it should stand, and without reason omitted, since it is found in the parallel places in Matthew and in the first epistle to the Corinthians.

Ellicott and Robertson compare the accounts and fix the terms. Ellicott notes that Mark agrees with Matthew in using the word ‘blessing’ of the bread and ‘giving thanks’ of the cup, while Luke uses the latter word of the bread and implies by his ‘likewise’ that the same form was repeated over the cup; and he corrects the tense of the clause about the blood, since the participle both here and in Matthew is present, so that the sense is ‘is being shed’. Robertson takes the cup to have contained the ordinary wine of the country mixed with two parts of water, and observes that the word for wine is not used here in the Gospels at all but the phrase ‘the fruit of the vine’; he adds that Mark and Matthew give substantially the same account of the institution, while Luke agrees closely with the account Paul says he received.

Theophylact, Chrysostom and Cyril of Jerusalem all take the sacrament realistically, though at different points. Theophylact denies that the bread is a mere figure of the Body of Christ and holds that it is changed into the very Body, on the ground that the Lord said the bread he gives is his flesh; that flesh, he adds, is veiled from our eyes on account of our weakness, since bread and wine are what we are used to. Chrysostom locates the agency rather than the substance: Christ is close to us even now, and he who prepared that table himself also consecrates it, for it is not man who makes the offerings to be the Body and Blood of Christ but Christ who was crucified for us — the words being spoken by the mouth of the priest and consecrated by the power and grace of God, the offerings consecrated by the word ‘This is my Body’. Cyril of Jerusalem argues from Paul’s account rather than from the Gospel text, holding that the teaching of the blessed Paul is of itself sufficient to give full assurance concerning the divine mysteries, by which those who have been deemed worthy become of the same body and blood with Christ.

Bede, Pseudo-Jerome and Gregory take the transition, the figure and the thanksgiving. Bede marks the passage from the old rite to the new: when the rites of the old Passover were finished the Lord passed to the new, in order to substitute the sacrament of his own Body and Blood for the flesh and blood of the lamb, and he took bread to show that he is the person to whom the Lord swore that he should be a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedec. Pseudo-Jerome reads the elements mystically: the Lord transfigures into bread his Body, which is the present Church, received in faith, blessed in its number, broken in its sufferings, given in its examples and taken in its doctrines; and he forms his Blood in a chalice of water and wine mingled together, that by the one we may be purged from our sins and by the other redeemed from their punishment. Gregory fastens on the thanksgiving offered with the Passion at hand: he who took upon himself the stripes of other men’s wickedness, and who had done nothing worthy of smiting, humbly gave a blessing in his suffering — which shows what each of us should do when beaten for his own sins, seeing that Christ bore calmly the stripes due to the sins of others.

debates: What the bread and cup become. Theophylact denies that the bread is a mere figure and asserts a change into the very Body; Chrysostom presses the consecrating agency, that Christ and not the priest makes the offerings what they are; Cyril of Jerusalem holds that communicants become of the same body and blood with Christ; Calvin and Henry both describe the rite by reference to the death remembered and the assurance given, without any language of change. This is the widest doctrinal separation in the chapter, and none of the witnesses engages the others directly.

Which word belongs to which element. Ellicott sets out the distribution — Mark and Matthew using ‘blessed’ of the bread and ‘gave thanks’ of the cup, Luke reversing it — and treats Luke’s ‘likewise’ as implying repetition of the same form.
Whether ‘eat’ belongs to the text. Clarke reports the omission in many manuscripts and versions and rejects it, resting on the parallels in Matthew and Paul.
What was in the cup. Robertson says the ordinary wine of the country mixed with two parts water, and notes that the text avoids the word for wine in favour of ‘the fruit of the vine’.
outliers: Gregory alone comments on the thanksgiving itself as an act of the sufferer, turning Christ’s blessing under the shadow of the Passion into a rule for those who suffer justly for their own faults.

Pseudo-Jerome alone identifies the bread with the Church rather than with the body of Christ, and works the identification through five clauses — received, blessed, broken, given and taken — that describe the Church’s life rather than the sacrament.
themes: the old Passover giving way to the new
a priest after the order of Melchizedec
change or figure in the elements
the blood of the new testament
the supper as memorial and assurance

26.pericope_label: And when they had sung an hymn, they went out into the mount of Olives. And Jesus saith unto them, All ye shall be offended because of me this night: for it is written, I will smite the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered. But after that I am risen, I will go before you into Galilee. But Peter said unto him, Although all shall be offended, yet will not I. And Jesus saith unto him, Verily I say unto thee, That this day, even in this night, before the cock crow twice, thou shalt deny me thrice. But he spake the more vehemently, If I should die with thee, I will not deny thee in any wise. Likewise also said they all.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin cover the narrative and its omissions. Gill identifies the hymn as the Hallel used at the Passover, places Christ’s words as spoken while they were going to the mount of Olives, observes that he assures them of his rising for their comfort though they would be offended and discouraged at his seizing, condemnation and crucifixion, and explains Peter’s protest as the reaction of a man greatly moved at being told that all of them would be offended that night and scattered from him and from one another. Calvin remarks on what the three Evangelists leave out: the discourses which John relates as delivered both in the house and on the road are absent here, because the object of these writers was rather to embrace the history of our Lord’s actions than his doctrine, so that they glance only at the fact that he went out of his own accord to the place where Judas was to come.

Wesley explains the double time-note in the prediction. The Jews reckoned their days beginning with the evening, according to the Mosaic computation which called the evening and the morning the first day; so that what is here called ‘this night’ after sunset is in the following verse called ‘this day’. He finds the accumulation peculiarly significant: Peter, confident as he is, will fail today, within four and twenty hours — indeed this very night, before ever the sun is risen. Clarke reinforces the same point from the manuscripts, noting that the pronoun for ‘thou’ is added by a large number of copies and versions and adds much to the energy of the passage, every word of which is deeply emphatical.

Lightfoot approaches the hymn through the rabbinic distinction between the Passover of the first month and that of the second. In the first, every man is bound under the law that leaven shall not be seen nor found among you, and is bound also to a hymn when he eats the Passover; in the second, leaven and unleavened bread may both be with a man in his house, and the obligation differs accordingly. Ellicott handles the disputed word in the prediction: ‘twice’ is omitted in many manuscripts, but it agrees with the emphatic mention of the cock crowing a second time later in the chapter and with the form of the prediction reported there, and may fairly be regarded as the true reading, the omission in some copies being accidental. On Peter’s reply he observes that the Greek tense implies frequent and continuous speaking.

Theophylact draws two lessons from the singing. Since they returned thanks before they drank and returned thanks again after drinking, we are taught to give thanks both before and after our food. And the singing itself, offered by one about to be betrayed, shows that he was glad to die for us, since when the betrayal was at hand he deigned to praise God — which teaches us in turn what we should do when we fall into troubles for the sake of the salvation of many.

Bede, Pseudo-Jerome and Augustine take the hymn, the place and the difficulty about the cock. Bede suggests the hymn may be the one recorded in John, which the Lord sang in returning thanks to the Father and in which he prayed with raised eyes for himself, for his disciples, and for those who should believe through their word; and he reads the departure typologically, finding it beautiful that the Lord should lead his disciples out to the mount of Olives once they had tasted his sacraments, to show that through the reception of the sacraments we ought to rise to higher gifts of virtue. Pseudo-Jerome takes the hymn as the praise of the Lord, quoting the psalm that the poor shall eat and be satisfied and they that seek the Lord shall praise him, and notes that Jesus is held captive on the very mount from which he ascended, so that we may know that we ascend to heaven from the place in which we watch and pray. Augustine addresses the apparent disagreement between the Evangelists: all say the Lord foretold that Peter would deny him before the cock crew, but Mark alone relates the matter more minutely, and some from inattention suppose him to differ from the rest. His answer rests on the denial being threefold — had the whole of it begun only after the cock crew, the other three would seem to have spoken falsely in saying he would deny thrice before the cock crew.

debates: Which hymn was sung. Gill names the Hallel used at the Passover; Bede proposes instead the prayer recorded in John; Pseudo-Jerome leaves it as the praise of the Lord generally and supports it from the Psalms; Lightfoot treats the obligation to sing as a point of Passover law rather than identifying the hymn.

Whether Mark’s account of the cockcrow contradicts the others. Augustine alone raises and answers it, arguing from the threefold structure of the denial that neither a wholly pre-cockcrow nor a wholly post-cockcrow reading can satisfy all four Evangelists; the rest pass the difficulty by.

Why the Synoptic account is so bare here. Calvin explains it from the purpose of the three, who set out to record actions rather than discourse, and notes that they mention only that Christ went out of his own accord to the place Judas would come to.

What ‘this day’ and ‘this night’ mean together. Wesley resolves the apparent doubling by the Jewish reckoning of the day from evening, and reads the piling up of terms as pressing how little time Peter’s confidence had left.
outliers: Theophylact alone turns the timing of the thanksgiving into a rule of table practice, arguing from grace before and after the cup to grace before and after ordinary food.
Bede alone reads the walk to the mount of Olives as a figure of what should follow communion, namely a rising to higher gifts of virtue.
themes: harmonising the accounts of the denial

32.pericope_label: And they came to a place which was named Gethsemane: and he saith to his disciples, Sit ye here, while I shall pray. And he taketh with him Peter and James and John, and began to be sore amazed, and to be very heavy; And saith unto them, My soul is exceeding sorrowful unto death: tarry ye here, and watch. And he went forward a little, and fell on the ground, and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass from him. And he said, Abba, Father, all things are possible unto thee; take away this cup from me: nevertheless not what I will, but what thou wilt. And he cometh, and findeth them sleeping, and saith unto Peter, Simon, sleepest thou? couldest not thou watch one hour? Watch ye and pray, lest ye enter into temptation. The spirit truly is ready, but the flesh is weak. And again he went away, and prayed, and spake the same words. And when he returned, he found them asleep again, (for their eyes were heavy,) neither wist they what to answer him. And he cometh the third time, and saith unto them, Sleep on now, and take your rest: it is enough, the hour is come; behold, the Son of man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. Rise up, let us go; lo, he that betrayeth me is at hand.

schools.summary: Gill explains the name of the place and the doubled address. Gethsemane lay at the foot of the Mount of Olives and was where the olives that grew in great plenty on the mount were pressed — and it was there, he adds, that our Lord began to be bruised for our sins. On the words spoken in prayer he notes that the first is Syriac and the second Greek, the one explaining the other, and offers as an alternative that the repetition expresses the vehemence of Christ’s affection and his strong confidence in God as his Father amid his distress, the Syriac version rendering it ‘Abba, my Father’.

Henry describes the nature of the agony. Christ is here entering upon his sufferings and begins with those that were the sorest of all, namely those in his soul; this agony in soul was the wormwood and the gall in the whole affliction and misery. From that Henry draws the point he wants: it appeared thereby that no sorrow was forced upon him, but that what he underwent was what he freely admitted.

Barnes, Ellicott, Robertson and Lightfoot work on the words. Barnes glosses the Aramaic term as denoting father, a Syriac word used by our Saviour as one of filial affection and tenderness. Ellicott notes that Mark uses a stronger word for Christ’s distress than Matthew’s ‘to be sorrowful’; that the record of ‘Abba’ as actually uttered is peculiar to Mark, with possible traces of the impression it made in the ‘Abba, Father’ of Romans and Galatians; and that where Matthew and Luke give the question to the sleeping disciples in the plural, Mark reports it in the singular and joins it to the emphatic utterance of the disciple’s name, his report including both the questions which appear separately in the other two Gospels. Robertson observes that Mark alone uses the verb for being greatly amazed, and that its cognate described the disciples’ amazement at the look of Jesus as he went toward Jerusalem, so that now Jesus himself feels amazement as he faces the struggle in the garden; on the address to God he holds that this is not a case of translation but of both terms used together with the article on each, as in Galatians, and suggests it may preserve a memory of Paul’s childhood prayers; and he notes that Christ uses the old name and not the new in waking Peter, whose boasted loyalty was already failing in the hour of crisis. Lightfoot distinguishes the two Semitic idioms, since the Hebrew form signifies a natural father but also a civil one — an elder, a master, a doctor, a magistrate — while the other denotes the natural relation only.

Clarke and Wesley take the address and the sleeper. Clarke glosses the Aramaic word as intimating filial affection and respect and parental tenderness, and holds that it seems to have been used by our Lord merely as man, to show his complete submission to his Father’s will and the tender affection he was conscious his Father had for him; he notes that the Syriac and Greek words for father stand joined here as they do in Paul. Wesley thinks Mark adds the Greek word by way of explication, and on the description of the agony says the original word imports the most shocking amazement mingled with grief, while the term rendered ‘sorrowful’ in the next verse intimates that Christ was surrounded with sorrow on every side, breaking in upon him with such violence as was ready to separate his soul from his body. Of the disciple he says only that it was to the zealous, the confident Peter that Christ spoke.

Theophylact explains both the solitude and the company. It was Christ’s custom always to pray by himself, in order to give us an example of seeking silence and solitude in our prayers. And in taking Peter, James and John he took only those who had been witnesses of his glory on Mount Tabor, so that they who had seen his glory might also see his sufferings, and might learn from his sorrow that he is really man.

Gloss, Bede, Pseudo-Jerome and Augustine take the setting and the condition. Gloss introduces the passage as the Evangelist’s account of a prayer supposed to have been offered for the disciples, the place being described first. Bede reports that Gethsemane is shown to this day at the foot of the Mount of Olives, gives its meaning as the valley of the fat or of fatness, and draws a contrast between Christ’s two places of prayer: praying on a mountain teaches us to ask for lofty things, while praying in the valley of fatness implies that humility and the fatness of interior love must be kept in our prayer. Pseudo-Jerome hears the psalm in the same phrase, that in the valley of fatness the fat bulls beset him, and finds a figure in the parting of the company, since those who are separated from Christ in his prayer are the same who are separated from him in his Passion — he prays while they sleep, overcome by the sloth of their heart. Augustine takes up the condition attached to the petition: Christ said not ‘if he could do it’ but ‘if it could be done’, since whatever he wills is possible, so that the condition must be understood as meaning ‘if he is willing’; and lest anyone suppose the Father’s power was being lessened, the words that immediately follow declare that all things are possible to him.

debates: What the name Gethsemane contributes. Bede derives it as the valley of fatness and builds a contrast with prayer on a mountain; Pseudo-Jerome hears in the same word the fat bulls of the psalm; Gill explains it from the olive presses and turns it into a figure of Christ being bruised.

Why the three were taken apart. Theophylact answers that they had seen the glory on Tabor and were now to see the sufferings, and so to learn his real manhood from his sorrow; Pseudo-Jerome takes the separation of the rest as anticipating their separation from him in the Passion.

What ‘Abba, Father’ is doing. Wesley and Gill treat the second word as explaining the first; Gill offers as an alternative that the doubling expresses vehemence of affection; Robertson denies that it is translation at all and takes both terms together as a fixed form, possibly remembered from Paul’s childhood; Ellicott traces its later use in the epistles; Lightfoot distinguishes the two Semitic words by whether they can bear a civil as well as a natural sense.

How the condition in the prayer is to be read. Augustine insists the words are ‘if it could be done’ rather than ‘if he could do it’, and construes the condition as concerning the Father’s will rather than his power, on the strength of the very next clause.
outliers: Bede alone contrasts the two locations of Christ’s prayer, mountain and valley, and reads them as teaching two different requirements of prayer — loftiness of aim and humility of spirit.

Ellicott alone tracks how Mark’s report of the rebuke differs in number and in fullness from the other two Gospels, noting that he alone addresses it to one disciple by name while combining both questions.
themes: the three who saw the glory
all things are possible unto thee
not what I will, but what thou wilt
the spirit ready, the flesh weak

43.pericope_label: And immediately, while he yet spake, cometh Judas, one of the twelve, and with him a great multitude with swords and staves, from the chief priests and the scribes and the elders. And he that betrayed him had given them a token, saying, Whomsoever I shall kiss, that same is he; take him, and lead him away safely. And as soon as he was come, he goeth straightway to him, and saith, Master, master; and kissed him. And they laid their hands on him, and took him. And one of them that stood by drew a sword, and smote a servant of the high priest, and cut off his ear. And Jesus answered and said unto them, Are ye come out, as against a thief, with swords and with staves to take me? I was daily with you in the temple teaching, and ye took me not: but the scriptures must be fulfilled. And they all forsook him, and fled. And there followed him a certain young man, having a linen cloth cast about his naked body; and the young men laid hold on him: And he left the linen cloth, and fled from them naked.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin handle the token and the fugitive. Gill explains that the sign was a common one in which the party had agreed, and on the young man canvasses the guesses: some think it was John, the youngest of the disciples, others James the Lord’s brother, others a young man of the house where Christ and the disciples had eaten the passover — but he concludes that the man does not seem to have been a disciple at all, since he is manifestly distinguished from those who all forsook Christ and fled. On the last verse he compares the leaving of the cloth to Joseph leaving his garment in the hands of his mistress. Calvin refuses to pursue the identification: he does not know how some have come to dream that it was John, nor does he think it of much importance to inquire; the chief point is to ascertain for what purpose Mark related the transaction, which he takes to be to show how those wicked men stormed, as men usually do in riotous assemblies.

Henry sets the seizure in the longer story. This was what Christ’s enemies had long aimed at, and they had often sent to take him, but he had escaped out of their hands because his hour was not yet come; nor could they have taken him now had he not freely surrendered himself. He notes the order of the suffering, that Christ began first to suffer in his soul and afterwards in his body.

Barnes, Ellicott, Robertson and Lightfoot supply the detail. Barnes holds it clear that the young man was not one of the apostles, thinks it probable he belonged to one of the neighbouring villages or houses and was roused from sleep by the noise the rabble made, and admits that it is not known why the circumstance is recorded by Mark, who alone has it. Ellicott notes that the incident is narrated by Mark only, that it had clearly made a deep impression on the minds of some of the disciples — probably enough on Peter’s — from whom the report came directly or indirectly, and that although some have supposed the young man to be Mark himself there is obviously no ground for it; on the order given to the crowd he corrects the rendering, since the word means seize. Robertson observes that Mark adds the scribes where John mentions Pharisees, and that the party was evidently a committee of the Sanhedrin, since Judas had made his bargain with that body; that the word for the agreed signal is common in ancient Greek for a concerted sign but occurs only here in the New Testament; that the instruction to lead him away safely is peculiar to Mark, Judas wishing no slip to occur; and that the incident of the young man is Mark’s alone, usually supposed to concern Mark himself, son of the Mary in whose house they had probably kept the passover, and a lifelike touch quite in keeping with the situation. Lightfoot argues from the Talmudists against the picture of a man snatching up bedclothes: the word is rightly rendered clothed in fine linen, and implies not that some linen had been loosely and by chance cast about him but that the garment in which he always went clothed was of linen.

Clarke and Wesley both reconstruct the scene at the end. Clarke supposes the young man was probably roused from sleep by the noise the rabble made in coming to apprehend Jesus, and having wrapped a sheet or some bed-clothing about him became the more conspicuous; on being seized he escaped by disengaging himself from the only thing they had hold of. Wesley tells the same story, that it does not appear the man was one of Christ’s disciples, and that hearing an unusual noise he started out of bed not far from the garden and ran out with only the sheet about him to see what was the matter; and he draws the contrast that the officers laid hold on one who was merely suspected of discipleship while they could not touch those who really were disciples. On the kiss Wesley suggests that our Lord in great condescension had, according to the Jewish custom, permitted his disciples to greet him so after they had been some time absent.

Theophylact explains why the traitor is described as one of the twelve. The phrase is not added without reason but to the greater conviction of the traitor, since although he was of the chief company among the disciples he turned himself to furious enmity against our Lord. On the sign agreed upon he remarks on the blindness of a man who supposed he could deceive Christ by a kiss.

Bede, Pseudo-Jerome and Gregory take the approach, the kiss and the fugitive. Bede has the Lord, after praying three times and obtaining by his prayers that the fear of the apostles should be amended by future repentance, go tranquil as to his Passion to meet his persecutors; and he observes that Judas still retained something of a disciple’s shame. Pseudo-Jerome states the principle behind the armed crowd — he who despairs of help from God has recourse to the power of the world — and sets the kiss given as a token beside Cain’s crafty and reprobate sacrifice, identifying Christ with the Joseph who was sold by his brethren and into whose soul the iron entered. Gregory contributes a single identification, that the young man who fled was John, who although he afterwards returned to the cross to hear the words of the Redeemer was at first frightened and fled.

debates: Who the young man was. Gregory says John outright; Calvin calls that a dream and declines to inquire; Gill lists John, James the Lord’s brother and a young man of the house, then rules out any disciple on the ground that the text distinguishes him from those who fled; Robertson reports the usual view that it was Mark himself; Ellicott records the same suggestion and says there is no ground for it; Barnes, Clarke and Wesley all take him for a stranger roused from sleep nearby.

What the linen cloth implies. Clarke, Barnes and Wesley build their reconstruction on bedclothes snatched up in haste; Lightfoot denies the premise from rabbinic evidence, holding that the word denotes the linen garment the man habitually wore rather than anything cast about him by chance. The two readings cannot both stand.

Why Mark records the incident at all. Barnes admits it is not known; Ellicott traces it to a deep impression left on a disciple, probably Peter; Calvin makes it evidence of the rioters’ violence; Robertson treats it as autobiographical.

What ‘one of the twelve’ adds here. Theophylact takes it as aggravating the guilt by contrast with Judas’s standing; Bede finds a remnant of shame in the man; Pseudo-Jerome compares the kiss to Cain’s sacrifice.
outliers: Lightfoot alone approaches the fleeing young man through Jewish dress rather than through the question of his identity, and his conclusion undercuts the reconstruction the other moderns share.

Henry alone frames the arrest as something Christ permitted rather than suffered, observing that earlier attempts had failed because his hour was not come and that this one succeeded only by his surrender.
themes: a multitude with swords and staves
the sword and the servant’s ear
they all forsook him and fled
the young man in the linen cloth

53.pericope_label: And they led Jesus away to the high priest: and with him were assembled all the chief priests and the elders and the scribes. And Peter followed him afar off, even into the palace of the high priest: and he sat with the servants, and warmed himself at the fire. And the chief priests and all the council sought for witness against Jesus to put him to death; and found none. For many bare false witness against him, but their witness agreed not together. And there arose certain, and bare false witness against him, saying, We heard him say, I will destroy this temple that is made with hands, and within three days I will build another made without hands. But neither so did their witness agree together.

schools.summary: Gill supplies the identifications and the sense of the failure. The high priest is Caiaphas, as the Syriac, Arabic and Persic versions add, and this followed the taking and binding and the visit to Annas, who sent him bound to Caiaphas. Another disciple, perhaps John, also followed, having recovered somewhat from the fright, and went in along with Jesus, Peter afterwards getting in by his means; both kept at a distance that they might not be observed and exposed to danger. Gill notes that the chief priests especially were the most busy and active in the matter, that the word “false” is not expressed in the Syriac, Persic and Ethiopic versions, and that the witnesses were obliged to stand while they gave in their testimony. On the last verse he is precise: their witness did agree in that both testified the same thing, but it was not equal, not answerable to their desires nor sufficient to convict him of a capital crime for which they could condemn him to death.

Henry frames the whole as an arraignment, trial, conviction and condemnation in the ecclesiastical court, before the great sanhedrim of which the high priest was president — the same Caiaphas who had lately adjudged it expedient that Christ should be put to death, guilty or not guilty, and who might therefore justly be excepted against as partial. He notes the state Caiaphas kept in his palace, and that in the dead of night all the chief priests, elders and scribes who were in the secret were assembled, ready to receive the prey, so sure were they of it. Peter followed at a distance, his late courage dwindled into such cowardice, and when he came to the palace he sneakingly went and sat with the servants that he might not be suspected of belonging to Christ — no proper place and no proper company for Peter, but his entrance into a temptation. On the evidence Henry observes that they had seized him as a malefactor and then had no indictment to prefer, so they sought witnesses, pumping some with ensnaring questions, offering bribes to others, endeavouring to frighten others; that the chief priests and elders were by Deuteronomy entrusted with prosecuting false witnesses and were now ringleaders in the crime; and that the two accounts differ, one swearing that he said he was able to destroy the temple and build it in three days, the other that he would destroy this temple made with hands and build another made without hands, so that their testimony was not sufficient nor equal to the charge of a capital crime.

Clarke and Wesley add short notes. Clarke refers the denial to Matthew and observes that the phrase is literally at the light, a fire casting considerable light, in consequence of which the maidservant was the better able to distinguish him. Wesley calls it an amazing proof of the overruling providence of God, considering both their authority and the rewards they could offer, that no two consistent witnesses could be procured to charge him with any gross crime; renders the failure as “were not equal,” not equal to the charge of a capital crime; and notes that the words thus misrepresented had been spoken at least three years before, so that their going back so far to find matter for the charge was a glorious though silent attestation of the unexceptionable manner in which he had behaved through the whole course of his public ministry.

Barnes offers only cross-references here; Ellicott, Robertson and Lightfoot carry the span. Ellicott prefers “was sitting and warming himself” and “with the officers,” and notes that the phrase is literally at the light, the word bringing out vividly the effect of the glare of the charcoal fire on Peter’s face; that Mark gives what Matthew only implies as the cause of the failure; that Mark is here less definite than Matthew, who wrote for Jews and was anxious to show that the rule requiring two or three witnesses had barely been complied with; that “this temple” is the word indicating the sanctuary or shrine; that the made-with-hands antithesis is peculiar to Mark though perhaps echoed in the “more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands” of Hebrews; and that we are not told in what respects the evidence failed to agree, possibly in details of time and place. Robertson observes that Mark uses the constative aorist where Matthew and Luke have the picturesque imperfect, possibly not caring to dwell on Peter furtively following at a distance, not bold enough to take an open stand as the Beloved Disciple did yet unable to remain away; that the periphrastic imperfect pictures Peter making himself at home with the officers, literally under-rowers; that since John describes him standing he probably did now one and now the other in his restless weary mood; and that fire has light as well as heat, so that he was not hidden as much as he supposed. On the evidence Robertson notes that the testimonies were not equal, not corresponding on essential points, that no two witnesses bore joint testimony as Deuteronomy required, and that the imperfects indicate repeated failures; he allows that a real saying of Jesus may underlie the perversion, and quotes Swete that Jesus did in fact do what he is quoted as saying, his death destroying the old order and his resurrection creating the new, though the witnesses did not mean that. Lightfoot sets out the traditional canons, which divided testimony into three parts — a vain testimony, which once heard is set aside as speaking nothing to the business; a standing testimony, which though it did not prove the matter beyond doubt was not rejected but admitted to examination by citation, others being allowed to disprove it; and the testimony of words that agreed together, an even evidence — and remarks that had they examined by that exact search and scrutiny the witnesses who babbled and barked against Christ, envy and madness itself could not have fastened any crime upon him.

Theophylact explains the plural title and the prejudged verdict. Though the law commanded that there should be but one high priest, there were then many put into the office and stripped of it year by year by the Roman emperor; he therefore calls chief priests those who had finished the time allotted to them and had been stripped of their priesthood. Their actions, he says, are a sign of their judgment, which they carried on as they had prejudged it, for they sought for a witness that they might seem to condemn and destroy Jesus with justice. On the alleged saying he notes that the Lord had not said “I will destroy” but “Destroy,” nor “made with hands” but “this temple.”

The Gloss, Bede and Pseudo-Jerome cover the whole span. The Gloss marks the transition, that the evangelist has related how the Lord was taken by the servants of the priests and now begins to relate how he was condemned to death in the house of the high priest. Bede identifies the high priest as Caiaphas, who as John writes was high priest that year and of whom Josephus relates that he bought his priesthood of the Roman Emperor; he judges it right that the man about to deny should follow afar off, since he could not have denied Christ if he had remained close to him; and on the fire he distinguishes the fire of charity, of which it is said “I am come to send fire on the earth,” from the fire of covetousness, holding that this fire, raised in the hall of Caiaphas by the suggestion of an evil spirit, armed the tongues of the traitors, and that a fire lit amid the cold of night figured what the wicked assembly was doing within, since because of the abounding of iniquity the love of many waxes cold — Peter, benumbed for a time by that cold, wished to be warmed at the coals of Caiaphas’s servants because he sought the consolation of worldly comfort in the society of traitors. On the charge Bede notes that the Lord had said “I will raise up,” meaning a thing with life and soul, a breathing temple, and defines the offence: he is a false witness who understands words in a sense in which they are not spoken. Pseudo-Jerome opens with the gathering together of the bulls among the heifers of the people, says of Peter that though fear holds him back love draws him on, and allegorises the scene — the hall of the high priest is the enclosure of the world, the servants are the devils, with whom whoever remains cannot weep for his sins, and the fire is the desire of the flesh. He adds that iniquity lied as the queen did against Joseph and the priests against Susannah, but a flame goes out if it has no fuel; that whatever is not consistent is held to be doubtful; and that it is usual with heretics to extract the shadow out of the truth, since the Lord did not say what they said but something like it, of the temple of his body, which he raised again after two days.

debates: How the fire in the hall should be read. Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson keep to the physical fact, that the word means light and the charcoal glare exposed Peter’s face; Bede makes it a figure of the cold love of the wicked assembly and of Peter seeking worldly comfort among traitors; Pseudo-Jerome makes the hall the world, the servants devils, and the fire the desire of the flesh.

Why the testimony failed. Gill and Wesley take the word to mean not equal to a capital charge; Robertson appeals to the legal requirement of two agreeing witnesses and to Mark’s repeated imperfects; Henry locates the discrepancy between the two versions of the temple saying; Ellicott says the cause is left unstated; Lightfoot measures the proceeding against the rabbinic grades of evidence.

What was wrong with the reported saying. Theophylact says the imperative was turned into a first person and “this temple” into “made with hands”; Bede says a false witness is one who takes words in a sense in which they were not spoken; Pseudo-Jerome that heretics extract the shadow from the truth; Robertson allows a genuine saying underneath and cites Swete that the event proved it true.

Why there were several chief priests. Theophylact explains it from the Roman practice of installing and deposing annually, so that the title covers men out of office; Bede reports from Josephus that Caiaphas bought the office from the emperor; Gill simply names him from the versions.
outliers: Lightfoot alone judges the trial by the sanhedrim’s own rules of evidence rather than by the gospel narrative, and concludes that the court’s procedure, properly applied, would itself have acquitted the prisoner.
Wesley alone turns the collapse of the prosecution into a positive testimony, arguing that the need to reach back three years for a charge is itself evidence of an unexceptionable ministry.
themes: led away to the high priest
made with hands and without hands

60.pericope_label: And the high priest stood up in the midst, and asked Jesus, saying, Answerest thou nothing? what is it which these witness against thee? But he held his peace, and answered nothing. Again the high priest asked him, and said unto him, Art thou the Christ, the Son of the Blessed? And Jesus said, I am: and ye shall see the Son of man sitting on the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds of heaven. Then the high priest rent his clothes, and saith, What need we any further witnesses? Ye have heard the blasphemy: what think ye? And they all condemned him to be guilty of death. And some began to spit on him, and to cover his face, and to buffet him, and to say unto him, Prophesy: and the servants did strike him with the palms of their hands.

schools.summary: Gill supplies the court arrangement and short glosses. Standing up in the midst means in the midst of the sanhedrim, of which he was now president: he sat at the head, the father of the council at his right hand, and the rest of the council before him in a semicircle, like the half of a round corn floor, so that they were all before him and he in the middle right against them. Christ held his peace knowing it would be to no purpose, and signifying thereby that the things alleged against him were unworthy of an answer. On the confession Gill supplies the sense, that “I am” means the Son of God, in proof of which he adds what follows. The high priest rent his clothes as was usual upon hearing blasphemy, which he now supposed the case, or at least would have it so thought. Gill notes that the Arabic renders it the manifest blasphemy and the Syriac adds “out of his own mouth,” and that those who began to spit on him were the men that held him, fulfilling prophecy.

Henry carries the narrative. The high priest stood up in a heat under pretence of justice but really to ensnare him, and Christ still answered nothing, to set us an example of patience under calumnies, since when we are reviled we are not to revile again, and of prudence, since a man may be made an offender for a word and our defence made our offence, so that it is an evil time indeed when the prudent must keep silence lest they make bad worse and commit their cause to him that judgeth righteously. When asked whether he was the Christ he confessed and denied not; Henry notes from Hammond that the Jews when they named God generally added blessed for ever, so that the Blessed is a peculiar title of God, and that for proof of his being the Son of God Christ binds them over to his second coming — the Son of man who now appears so mean and despicable, whom they trample upon, they shall shortly see and tremble before. He marvels that such a word, spoken with a grandeur not agreeable to his present appearance, did not amount in the opinion of any of them to an arrest of judgment, as Felix trembled and adjourned the trial when Paul reasoned of the judgment to come; but they were so blinded with malice that like the horse rushing into battle they mocked at fear. On the rending Henry reports that some take the word for the pontifical vestments, and holds that as Saul’s rending of Samuel’s mantle signified the rending of the kingdom from him, much more did this signify the rending of the priesthood from Caiaphas, while Christ’s clothes even at the crucifixion were kept entire, since when the Levitical priesthood was done away this man, because he continues ever, has an unchangeable priesthood. The question “What think ye?” seemed fairly put but was really prejudged, since the high priest had already said “Ye have heard the blasphemy,” giving judgment first when as president of the court he ought to have voted last; what friends Christ had in the sanhedrim did not appear, and probably they had no notice. Of the abuse Henry says it seems some of the priests themselves so far forgot the dignity and duty of their place as to help their servants play the fool with a condemned prisoner, making their diversion of it while they waited for the morning to complete their villainy, and making a merry night of the night of observations.

Clarke alone speaks here, on the text of the high priest’s question. He renders it “of God the blessed one,” noting that the word for God is added by a number of manuscripts, the Vulgate and one of the Itala, and might be introduced into the text in italics if the authority of the manuscripts and versions be not deemed sufficient; it appears necessary for the better understanding of the text, though the adjective conveys a good sense by itself, according to a frequent Hebrew form of speech.

Barnes gives cross-references only; Ellicott and Robertson supply the philology. Ellicott observes that Matthew and Luke have simply “the Son of God” where Mark has “the Son of the Blessed,” the use of the Blessed as a name of God in doxologies and other solemn formulae being a common practice; that Mark uses the word for the inner garment where Matthew uses that for the outer; that the translators’ “guilty of death” follows the old English usage connecting guilty with the punishment a man is liable to rather than with the crime; and that the covering of the face, recorded by Mark and Luke but not by Matthew, gave point to the taunt “Prophesy,” since they blindfolded the Prophet and then called on him to use his power of supernatural vision — the two forms of outrage, with the clenched fist and with the open palm, being specified by both Matthew and Mark.
