Robertson notes that the high priest arose for greater solemnity, to make up by bluster the lack of evidence, stepping into the midst as if to attack Jesus by vehement questions; that Mark adds a negative statement to the positive “kept silent” and does not give the solemn oath recorded in Matthew; that where Matthew has “Thou hast said,” the equivalent of the affirmative, Mark’s “I am” is definite beyond controversy; that “they all” would mean Joseph of Arimathea was not present, since he did not consent to the death of Jesus, and that Nicodemus was apparently absent also, probably not invited because of previous sympathy, but that all who were present voted for the death; that the word for covering the face means to put a veil around it, translated blindfolded in Luke; that the officers are the same as in the earlier verse, those who had arrested Jesus and still held him; and that the verb originally meant to smite with a rod but in late writers came to mean to slap the face with the palm, a sixth-century papyrus using the substantive for a scar on the face resulting from a blow, while Swete suggests “they caught him with blows” and rods remain possible since lictors carried them.

Theophylact and Cyril of Jerusalem take different parts. Theophylact says the Lord remained silent because he knew they would not attend to his words, as Luke has it, “If I tell you, ye will not believe”; that the high priest put his question not that he might learn and believe but to seek occasion against him; and that he asks “the Son of the Blessed” because there were many christs, that is anointed persons such as kings and high priests, but none of these was called the Son of the Blessed God, the Ever-praised. He explains why Jesus answered though he knew they would not believe: lest they should afterwards say that if they had heard anything from him they would have believed, so that this is their condemnation, that they heard and did not believe. Theophylact takes “power” as a name for the Father, and insists that the Lord will not come without a body but will appear in the judgment as he appeared to those who crucified him. On the rent clothes he says the high priest does after the manner of the Jews, who rent their clothes whenever anything intolerable or sad occurred, and did so here to show that Christ had spoken great and intolerable blasphemy; and that the Jewish priesthood was to be rent from the time they condemned Christ as guilty of death. Cyril of Jerusalem does not treat the trial but uses the saying as a testimony to the Son’s sitting at the right hand of the Father, adducing the parallel in Matthew, the words of the Apostle Peter that Christ is on the right hand of God having gone into heaven, the statement to the Romans that it is Christ that died, yea rather that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God, and the charge to the Ephesians concerning the working of his mighty power wrought in Christ when he raised him from the dead.

Bede, Pseudo-Jerome, Augustine and Leo divide the span. Bede holds that the more Jesus remained silent before the false witnesses, who were unworthy of his answer, and before the impious priests, the more the high priest, overcome with anger, endeavoured to provoke him to answer that he might find room for accusing him from anything whatever he might say; and that the high priest, angry and impatient at finding no room for accusation, rises from his seat, showing by the motion of his body the madness of his mind. He turns the confession on the scorner: if the contempt, weakness and cross in Christ are a subject of scorn to Jew, pagan and heretic, see how by this the Son of Man is to sit at the right hand of the Father and to come in his majesty on the clouds of heaven. On the rent clothes he finds a higher mystery, that in the Passion the Jewish priest rent his own ephod while the garment of the Lord could not be rent even by the soldiers who crucified him — a figure that the Jewish priesthood was to be rent on account of the wickedness of the priests, whereas the solid strength of the Church, often called the garment of her Redeemer, can never be torn asunder; and he reads the taunt “Prophesy” as an insult aimed at one who wished to be looked upon as a prophet by the people. Pseudo-Jerome opens with the Saviour led as a sheep to the slaughter without crying, mute and keeping silence yea even from good words, and calls the silence of Christ the pardon for the defence or excuse of Adam; the priests looked from afar for him whom though near they could not see, as Isaac in his blindness did not know Jacob under his hands yet prophesied what should come. He says Jesus answered “I am” that they might be inexcusable; that the high priest asks concerning the Son of God while Jesus answers concerning the Son of Man, so that we may understand the Son of God to be also the Son of Man and make no quaternity in the Trinity, but let man be in God and God in man; that sitting on the right hand of power means reigning in life everlasting and in the divine power; and that as he ascended in a cloud he will come with a cloud, having ascended in that body alone which he took of the Virgin and returning to judgment with the whole Church, which is his body and his fulness. They condemned him guilty of death, he adds, that by his guiltiness he might absolve our guilt; and each indignity is a remedy — by being spit upon he washes the face of our soul, by the covering of his face takes the veil from our hearts, by the buffets dealt on his head heals the head of mankind, that is Adam, and by the blows of the hands earns that great praise testified by the clapping of our hands and by our lips. Augustine observes that Matthew does not say Jesus answered “I am” but “Thou hast said,” and that Mark shows the words to be equivalent; and he notes that the Lord suffered these things until morning in the house of the high priest, whither he had first been brought. Leo says that Caiaphas, to increase the odiousness of what they had heard, rent his clothes, and without knowing what his frantic action meant deprived himself by that madness of the honour of the priesthood, forgetting the command that the high priest shall not uncover his head or rend his clothes.

debates: Why the silence, and why it ended. Bede holds the witnesses unworthy of an answer; Gill that a reply would have been to no purpose; Pseudo-Jerome makes the silence itself the pardon of Adam’s excuse; Henry makes it an example of patience and prudence; Theophylact alone explains the speech that followed, that he answered lest they plead they had never heard.

Whether Mark’s ‘I am’ is Matthew’s ‘Thou hast said.’ Augustine says Mark shows the two equivalent; Robertson grants the equivalence but calls Mark’s form definite beyond controversy and notes that Mark drops Matthew’s adjuration.

What the rending of the clothes signified. Gill and Theophylact take it as the customary act on hearing blasphemy; Ellicott notes only that Mark names the inner garment and Matthew the outer; Henry and Bede read it as a figure of the priesthood being rent away, contrasted with the Lord’s unrent garment; Leo makes it a breach of the law of Leviticus by which Caiaphas deposed himself.

How the abuse should be read. Ellicott and Robertson reconstruct it physically, from the blindfold that gave the taunt its point to the difference between fist and open palm; Bede takes the taunt as aimed at his prophetic claim; Pseudo-Jerome assigns each indignity a remedial effect on a part of fallen man.
outliers: Cyril of Jerusalem alone treats the words as a proof text rather than as testimony at a trial, collecting the apostolic statements of the session at the right hand and leaving the scene entirely out of view.
Leo alone turns the high priest’s gesture against himself, arguing from the Levitical prohibition that the act which was meant to condemn Christ in fact stripped Caiaphas of his office.

66.pericope_label: And as Peter was beneath in the palace, there cometh one of the maids of the high priest: And when she saw Peter warming himself, she looked upon him, and said, And thou also wast with Jesus of Nazareth. But he denied, saying, I know not, neither understand I what thou sayest. And he went out into the porch; and the cock crew. And a maid saw him again, and began to say to them that stood by, This is one of them. And he denied it again. And a little after, they that stood by said again to Peter, Surely thou art one of them: for thou art a Galilaean, and thy speech agreeth thereto. But he began to curse and to swear, saying, I know not this man of whom ye speak. And the second time the cock crew. And Peter called to mind the word that Jesus said unto him, Before the cock crow twice, thou shalt deny me thrice. And when he thought thereon, he wept.

schools.summary: Gill supplies the topography and the versions. Peter was beneath in the palace, not at the lower and further end of the room but in the lower part of it, that part where Jesus and the sanhedrim were being upon advanced ground with steps ascending to it; and the maid saw him warming himself at the fire in the midst of the hall. On the second challenge Gill notes that the Syriac and Persic read “that maid,” the selfsame maid as before, while the Arabic makes it another and the Ethiopic a daughter of the high priest. He glosses the denials as denying that he was with Jesus or a disciple of his, and the oath as wishing the most dreadful things upon himself and swearing by the living God. On the second crowing he notes that the Vulgate, Syriac and Ethiopic versions and one of Beza’s copies read that it followed immediately, and places it about three in the morning, which is what is properly called the cock crowing.

Henry anatomises the denial in stages. It began in keeping at a distance from Christ, for Peter had followed afar off and was now beneath in the palace at the lower end of the hall; those who are shy of Christ are in a fair way to deny him. It was occasioned by his associating with the high priest’s servants and sitting among them, and those who think it dangerous to be in company with Christ’s disciples, lest they be drawn in to suffer for him, will find it much more dangerous to be in company with his enemies, where they may be drawn in to sin against him. The temptation was that he was charged as a disciple, known for a Galilaean by his speaking broad; it does not appear that he was in danger of prosecution, only of being bantered and ridiculed — while the chief priests abused the Master the servants abused the disciples. All things considered the temptation could not be called formidable, being only a maid who casually cast her eye upon him, to whom he need have made no reply. The sin was great, since he denied Christ before men when he ought to have confessed him and appeared in court a witness for him; Christ had often given notice of his sufferings and had told them they must take up their cross, yet Peter was so afraid of suffering that he would lie and swear to avoid it, and having readily owned Christ when he was admired and flocked after, was ashamed of him now he was deserted and run down. But his repentance was speedy: he denied thrice, the third worst of all since he cursed and swore to confirm it, and that third blow, which might have stunned him, roused him. On the closing phrase Henry supplies several senses — he added to weep, making it a Hebraism; he continued weeping; he flung out and wept; he threw himself down and wept; he covered his face, casting his garment about his head that he might not be seen to weep; he cast his eyes upon his Master, who turned and looked upon him, which Dr. Hammond supplies as a probable conjecture; or, fixing his mind upon it, he wept, since it is not a transient thought of what is humbling that will suffice. Henry adds his own suggestion, that the word may mean his laying a load upon himself and throwing confusion into his own face, as the publican smote his breast in sorrow for sin. He observes that this evangelist, said to have written under Peter’s direction, speaks as fully of Peter’s sin as any of them but more briefly of his sorrow, which Peter in modesty would not have magnified.

Clarke and Wesley speak at the close. Clarke reports that the phrase may be rendered “he fell a weeping,” which Mr. Wakefield thinks comes nearest to the original; that others take it of the wrapping of his head in the skirts of his garment through shame and anguish; that others refer it rather to the violence or hurry with which he left the place, impelled by the terrors and remorse of his guilty conscience; and he concludes that our own translation is as good as any. Wesley, on the covering of the head, says it was a usual custom with mourners and was fitly expressive both of grief and shame.

Barnes gives cross-references only; Ellicott and Robertson carry the detail. Ellicott notes that the order of the words in the first challenge varies in the manuscripts, the better ones giving them with an emphatic scorn, “And thou also wast with the Nazarene, Jesus”; that the noun Mark uses for the porch is not the same as Matthew’s but signifies literally the space before the palace, the vestibule; that the second maid is better rendered “the maid,” the one who had pointed him out before; and that the clause about Peter’s speech agreeing thereto, natural as it seems, is wanting in many of the best manuscripts and may therefore have been an interpretative addition, possibly made by Mark himself in what we may call a revised edition of his Gospel. On the last verse he explains that the Greek word is a somewhat peculiar one meaning literally throwing at or on, that the English version assumes it to mean casting the mind or thoughts, just as to reflect is to bend the mind, and is probably right, and that although the margin gives two conjectures and another may be found in the idea that Peter cast himself down and wept, there is not enough authority for any other interpretation to justify a change in the text. Robertson takes “beneath in the court” to imply that Jesus was upstairs when the sanhedrim met, and holds Matthew’s “without in the court” equally true, the open court being outside the rooms and also below. He observes that Mark mentions the warming twice, as John does, so that Peter was twice beside the fire; that it is quite difficult to relate clearly the three denials as told in the four Gospels, since several may have joined in each time, both maids and men, one saying one thing and another another, and Matthew’s “the Galilean” answering to Mark’s “the Nazarene”; that the denial is fuller in Mark and briefest in John; that the word for the porch occurs only here in the New Testament, Plato using it of a prelude on a flute, and Matthew using instead a common word for a gate; that the crowing in the earlier verse is omitted by important witnesses and is genuine in the later verse where “the second time” also occurs, so that it may have crept in from there, Mark alone alluding to the twofold crowing; that the word for cursing comes from a root meaning an offering and then a thing devoted, Deissmann having found examples at Megara in the sense of curse, with the notion of calling down curses on oneself if the thing is not true; and that the participle in the last verse is used absolutely, the idiom involving the mind, Moulton quoting a Ptolemaic papyrus where it probably means to set to, while Mark’s inchoative imperfect “began to weep” stands against Matthew’s ingressive aorist, “burst into tears.”

Theophylact reads the fall as permitted and as precedent. The Lord allowed this to happen to Peter by his providence, lest he should be too much elated, and at the same time that he might prove himself merciful to sinners, as knowing from himself the result of human weakness. Peter was seized with fear and, forgetting the word of the Lord that whosoever shall confess him before men he will confess before his Father, denied him; but tears brought Peter by penitence to Christ. Theophylact then turns the case against a party: confounded be the Novatians, who say that he who sins after receiving baptism is not received to the remission of his sin, for behold Peter, who had also received the Body and Blood of the Lord, is received by penitence. The failings of saints are written, he concludes, that if we fall by want of caution we also may be able to run back by their example and hope to be relieved by penitence.

Augustine, Bede and Pseudo-Jerome share the span. Augustine observes that the evangelists do not relate the temptation of Peter in the same order: Luke first relates the temptation and then the injuries done to the Lord; John begins to speak of the temptation, then puts in some things concerning the ill-treatment, adds that he was sent from there to Caiaphas, and then goes back to unfold the temptation he had begun; while Matthew and Mark first notice the injuries and then the temptation. On the second challenge he holds that this maid is not the same but another, as Matthew says, and that in the second denial Peter was addressed by two persons, the maid whom Matthew and Mark mention and another of whom Luke takes notice. He argues from a comparison of all the evangelists that Peter had returned, since John says he denied him standing at the fire, so that the maid spoke not to Peter but to those who had remained when he went out, in such a way however that he heard it; coming back and standing again at the fire he contradicted them, so that the second denial was made not before the porch but within the palace at the fire, Matthew and Mark being silent as to his return for the sake of brevity. Bede asks what can be meant by his being first recognised by a woman, when men were more able to know him, unless it be that that sex might be seen to sin in the death of our Lord and that sex be redeemed by his Passion; he notes that the other evangelists do not mention this crowing of the cock, though they do not deny the fact, as some pass over in silence what others relate. He draws a lesson from the denial, that not only does he deny Christ who says that he is not the Christ, but he also who, although he is a Christian, denies himself to be such, since the Lord did not say “Thou shalt deny thyself to be my disciple” but “Thou shalt deny me.” On the Galilaean speech he explains that the Galilaeans did not speak a different tongue from the inhabitants of Jerusalem, both being Hebrews, but that each province and region has its own peculiarities and cannot avoid a vernacular pronunciation; and he remarks how hurtful it is to speak with the wicked, since Peter denied before infidels that he knew the Man whom among the disciples he had confessed to be God. He adds that Scripture is wont to point out a sacrament of the causes of things by the state of the time, so that Peter, who denied at midnight, repented at cock crow. Pseudo-Jerome says that Peter, when he had not the Spirit, yielded and lost courage at the voice of a girl, though with the Spirit he was not afraid before princes and kings; and in a mystical sense the first maid means the wavering, the second the assent, and the third man the act — the threefold denial which the remembrance of the word of the Lord washes away through tears. The cock crows for us, he adds, when some preacher stirs up our hearts by repentance to compunction; we begin to weep when we are set on fire within by the spark of knowledge, and we go forth when we cast out what we were within.

debates: How the four accounts of the denial fit together. Augustine works out the order and place, holding the second maid to be another person, two speakers to be involved, and Peter to have returned to the fire so that the second denial was inside the palace; Robertson concedes that the three denials cannot be related clearly at all, since several may have spoken each time; Gill finds the versions themselves split over whether the second maid is the first; Ellicott takes her for the same.

Whether the disputed clauses belong to the text. Robertson holds the first crowing an intrusion from the later verse, on the authority of weighty manuscripts; Ellicott suspects the clause about Peter’s speech on similar grounds, but allows that Mark himself may have added it in a revised edition; Bede, working from the Latin, treats the twofold crowing as fact and explains only why other evangelists omit it.

What the participle in the last verse means. Ellicott and Robertson take it of casting the mind upon the thing, Robertson adding papyrus evidence for ‘set to’; Clarke reports Wakefield’s ‘he fell a weeping’ and the rival guesses of a covered head and of a hurried exit, and declines to choose; Henry lists seven or eight supplies and adds a ninth of his own, that Peter laid a load upon himself; Wesley takes the covered head as the mourner’s custom.

What the fall teaches. Theophylact makes it a precedent for the readmission of the lapsed and turns it against the Novatians; Bede makes it a warning that a Christian who disowns his discipleship denies Christ himself; Theophylact and Pseudo-Jerome both trace it to weakness left unguarded, while Henry traces it to the prior step of keeping company with Christ’s enemies.
outliers: Pseudo-Jerome alone reads the three challengers as the successive stages of one sin — wavering, assent, act — and the cock as the preacher whose voice stirs the hearer to compunction, so that the narrative becomes a description of how any sin is committed and repented.
Theophylact alone puts the passage to controversial use, making Peter’s restoration a ruling in the dispute over post-baptismal sin rather than a lesson about Peter.
